turns.message:
You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

In your continual harness, entries created without global_=True belong to this session and are lost with it.

Continue same-color diagonal rays to blockers or grid edges For ARC grids with a uniform background and short colored segments, continue any diagonal segment formed by two or more same-color cells along its diagonal, extending the line in both directions as far as possible. Fill only background cells; stop at the grid edge or at any non-background cell, preserving existing colored cells (do not overwrite blockers). Repeated cells that are only horizontal or vertical do not trigger this rule. Example validated: a 7 pair on a NW-SE diagonal extended NW to the boundary; its SE continuation stopped at 8-colored cells. A 6 pair on NE-SW extended SW to the boundary and stopped NE at an 8. A diagonal 8 pair made no additions because it was blocked by 7 on one side and the edge on the other. Additional demos: a 9 diagonal ray continued along the diagonal; a vertical 6 pair and a nonmatching mixed-color pattern were unchanged.
ARC continue seeded diagonal color rays In sparse ARC grids, a pair of same-color cells on adjacent diagonal positions can seed a straight diagonal ray. Extend that color in the same direction through background cells until the grid edge or an occupied cell blocks it; preserve existing cells and other colors. Demos: (1) 5x16 background 4: color 1 at (2,9),(3,8) continued down-left by adding (4,7); a color-6 down-right pair at (0,8),(1,9) was blocked by a 7 at (2,10), so no overwrite. (2) 20x29 background 0: 9 at (1,12),(2,11) continued down-left to edge (13,0); 8 at (1,13),(2,14) continued down-right to edge (16,28). Solved 10x8 test: 4 at (1,2),(2,3) continued down-right with 4s at (3,4),(4,5),(5,6),(6,7). Coordinates are zero-based (row,column).
Periodic ARC grid: extend colored line residue pattern For this task family, a sparse set of colored straight lines encodes a periodic color pattern; complete zeros by repeating the pattern in the line-normal/phase coordinate. Infer the SMALLEST period p for which all clues at the same phase are consistent, then propagate the observed colors across the grid. For full-width horizontal bars, phase is row index mod p, and output repeats full-width rows vertically. Example: 25x25 bars at rows 4=3, 6=7, 17=9, 23=1: p=4 is the smallest collision-free period, mapping row residues 0=3, 1=9, 2=7, 3=1. For diagonal line clues slope +1, phase is (column-row) mod p; the output is the corresponding periodic diagonal-band tiling. Determine p by trying increasing positive periods and rejecting any that assign different observed colors to the same residue. Demonstrations: 13x13 horizontal stripes produced row period 7; 16x16 diagonal clues period 5; 26x26 diagonal clues period 8; 14x14 diagonal clues period 6. Preserve clue lines and fill missing residue classes consistently. Avoid guessing period from number of distinct colors alone: minimum compatible period worked for the solved horizontal case.
ARC periodic parallel stripe completion For ARC inputs made of parallel uniform stripes, complete the periodic pattern using stripe-line coordinates. Identify and ignore the background (often 0). Let P equal the number of foreground stripe lines, counting separate parallel line coordinates individually even if adjacent lines have the same color. A stripe at coordinate k assigns its color to phase k mod P; fill every line of the same orientation at that phase with the assigned color. Preserve the stripe orientation. For horizontal rows, k is the row index. For diagonal stripes in the demonstrated cases, k=r+c. Example: horizontal stripes at rows 0:4, 7:6, 9:2, 14:7 give P=4 and phases [0:4,1:2,2:7,3:6], so output rows repeat 4,2,7,6. Another horizontal example has background 0 and foreground rows 0:5, 2:2, 3:1, 4:9, 5:9, 6:9, 8:9; P=7, phases give [5,9,2,1,9,9,9], repeated. In that solved 9x9 test the 0 rows (1 and 7) were background, not foreground; count the seven nonzero rows to determine P.
Periodic ARC grid: phase selection examples and caution Observed examples for the periodic-line ARC task: output is a 2D periodic tiling where color is constant along each marked diagonal (down-right lines; class c-r mod p), or each full-width horizontal stripe (class row mod p). Choose the smallest p that avoids two different clue colors occupying one class. Horizontal stripe solved: p=4 for row clues 4:3, 6:7, 17:9, 23:1, giving residue colors [3,9,7,1]. The earlier guessed p=5 was incorrect, so use minimum compatible p, not unique-color-count+1. Diagonal demos confirmed periods 5 (14/16 grids), 6 (14 grid), and 8 (26 grid), from congruence of line offsets. If some residue classes lack a direct clue, do not assume a new color; examples fill a missing adjacent phase with the same color as a neighboring phase (e.g., p=5 demo had phase sequence [5,3,3,8,4]).
ARC line-fill between aligned markers For ARC line-fill tasks, preserve the input grid and all marker cells. In each row and each column, sort positions of the same marker color and recolor only cells strictly between consecutive aligned markers with color 3; never fill diagonal gaps or extend beyond endpoints. Apply horizontal and vertical intervals independently (a cell may be filled by either), keeping dimensions unchanged. The fill color is 3 even when marker/background colors vary. Confirmed on marker 0/background 2, marker 9/background 4, and marker 2/background 7. An earlier wrong attempt filled with the marker color; use 3. Also confirmed marker 6/background 0: fill color 3 strictly between consecutive same-color markers in rows and columns, preserving all original markers and dimensions. Additional confirmation: marker 1 on background 9 uses the same rule; with marker coordinates (0,6),(1,17),(2,11),(3,7),(3,15),(4,4),(4,9),(5,3),(5,11),(6,2),(6,9),(7,10),(7,11),(8,12),(8,18), fill color 3 lies only between aligned marker pairs in each row/column (e.g. row 3 columns 7–15 and column 11 rows 2–7), while all markers and background stay unchanged. Confirmed again for marker 0 on background 1 (task-2b954eea): output color 3 fills strict gaps between consecutive zeros along each row and column, preserves zero marker cells, leaves unfilled background as 1, and preserves grid dimensions.
ARC denoise rectangular color patches and remove stray pixels For ARC grids with a uniform background and several filled rectangular patches contaminated by isolated pixels of other colors, preserve each underlying rectangle and its color, replace anomalous cells inside the rectangle with its fill color, and reset stray pixels outside all rectangles to the background. Determine rectangle bounds from the larger, coherent same-color block, allowing single-cell defects on a boundary; do not absorb clearly protruding single pixels if including them would require adding a mostly empty row/column. Multiple differently colored rectangles may share rows and sit close together, so map each row/column carefully and do not omit one rectangle because another begins on the same row. In task-401c00a3, background 8; clean patches were color 6 at rows 0-1 cols 10-14, color 7 at rows 1-2 cols 0-2, color 0 at rows 4-6 cols 7-12 and rows 8-11 cols 4-9, color 7 at rows 13-15 cols 4-7, color 9 at rows 15-18 cols 10-14, color 6 at rows 20-24 cols 1-6, color 7 at rows 21-25 cols 10-14, and color 9 at rows 26-28 cols 1-3. All isolated markers outside these shapes reverted to 8. A first answer was wrong because it missed the third row (row 15) of the 7 rectangle where the adjacent 9 rectangle also begins; correcting that one row solved the task. Demonstrations confirm zero can be a patch color even when the background is nonzero, and in-patch marker colors are replaced by the rectangle color.
ARC periodic stripe completion from sparse parallel lines For ARC tasks where sparse colored cells form complete/partial parallel straight stripes and output fills the whole grid with repeated stripes: infer orientation from stripe direction, then extend periodic stripes across the grid. In observed examples: down-right diagonal stripes use invariant c-r; down-left/anti-diagonal stripes use invariant r+c; horizontal stripes use row index. The period can be the number of distinct stripe offsets represented in the input, with each stripe color assigned to its offset modulo that period. Map the color for each offset residue and tile across the grid. Examples: demo1 had 6 diagonal offset lines and output period 6; demo2 had 4 marked rows and output period 4; demo3 had 3 diagonal offsets (c-r=1=>2, 3=>3, -1=>5) and output period 3. In task-03e48a56, anti-diagonal stripe sums 2 and 28 were color7, sum33 color9; period=3 (number of distinct lines), so r+c mod3=0 ->9 and residues1,2 ->7. Important: choosing a smaller consistent period is not necessarily correct; period followed the count of distinct clue stripes in the confirmed examples (period2 was wrong on this case, period3 correct).
ARC periodic stripe tiling from sparse stripe clues For ARC tasks where the input contains sparse full-width horizontal stripes or diagonal stripes and the output expands them into a full periodic tiling: identify each distinct nonzero stripe as a clue, determine its stripe-coordinate (horizontal rows: row index; down-right diagonal: k=column-row), and use the number of distinct clue stripes as the period. Each clue fixes the color at its coordinate modulo that period; repeat those colors cyclically across the whole grid, filling every cell (no zeros). For horizontal rows, output is constant across each row. For down-right diagonals, output is constant on c-r diagonals, i.e. output[r][c]=motif[(c-r) mod period]. Example from task-03e48a56: clues are color 5 on c-r=-5 and color 6 on c-r=-10, so two stripes imply period 2; even k gets 6 and odd k gets 5, producing a checkerboard. Examples showed row-stripe clue counts 4, 6, and 8 yielding periods 4, 6, and 8, and a five-diagonal motif yielding period 5. The motif may include duplicate adjacent colors; preserve clue phase from actual coordinates.
Additional confirmed instance for task-03e48a56: a 2x2 diagonal-clue grid [[9,3],[0,9]] outputs [[9,3],[3,9]]. The clue at c-r=0 is 9 and at c-r=1 is 3; repeating the period-2 diagonal pattern fills the zero at c-r=-1 with 3.
ARC periodic background from sparse parallel lines Continual-ARC task-03e48a56 solved with a modular tiling rule. Infer a period/orientation from sparse colored diagonal-line clues, then fill the entire grid using repeating color classes. For the 27x27 test, lines were slope down-right (constant c-r): color 5 on c-r=6, color 1 on c-r=16 and c-r=-7. Modulo 3, these clues cover all classes: 5 where (c-r)%3=0, 1 on residues 1 and 2. Output is fully filled (no zeros): cell(r,c)=5 iff (c-r)%3==0, else 1. Confirmed correct.

Related demonstrations establish the general pattern: (1) a 10x10 grid with horizontal uniform rows at indices 3..9 colored 6,3,5,3,8,6,5 and blank rows 0..2; output repeats this 7-row sequence cyclically, backfilling the top as 8,6,5. (2) a 20x20 grid with sparse anti-diagonal clues (constant r+c) colored 9 at sums 31 and 36, and 3 at sum 38; output is a full periodic tiling: 3 where (r+c)%3==2, else 9. (3) a 14x14 grid with uniform row clues 4 at row 0, 6 at row 10, 3 at row 11; output repeats period 3 by row index: 4 for r%3==0, 6 for ==1, 3 for ==2. General lesson: sparse placements can encode a periodic color field along row/column/diagonal coordinates; infer the orientation from the clue lines, find the smallest consistent modulus, assign colors from clue residues, and repeat over the whole grid.
